title: Record-Breaking X-Ray Flash Could Be the Birth Cry of a Magnetar
summary:
When two neutron stars crash together, they usually announce it with a short, sharp burst of gamma rays — a flash that can vanish in under two seconds. But on July 4, 2025, astronomers saw something different: a bright X-ray flash that lingered for nearly 10 minutes. That's the longest-lasting X-ray signal ever linked to a neutron star merger, and it might be the first clear evidence of a magnetar being born.

Neutron stars are the incredibly dense cores left behind when massive stars die. They pack the mass of our Sun into a ball about the size of a city. When two of them merge, they send out gravitational waves and a burst of light. Usually, that light is a short gamma-ray burst. But if the crash leaves behind a magnetar — a rapidly spinning neutron star with an enormous magnetic field — it can keep pumping energy into the explosion, making it brighter and longer-lasting.

"When I saw the X-ray data from this new event, I realized something was up," said Eleonora Troja, a professor and co-author of the study published in Science Bulletin.

The event, called EP250704a/GRB 250704B, was first spotted by the Einstein Probe satellite, which launched in January 2024. Graduate student Niccolò Passaleva got the alert while traveling home by train. "All of a sudden I was rushing against time to commandeer one of the largest telescopes in the world from my laptop," he recalled. He and his team used the Very Large Telescope in Chile to measure the flash's redshift — a way to tell how far away it is. The result: z=0.6610, meaning the light traveled more than 6 billion years to reach us.

The team also checked for a supernova, which would be expected if a collapsing star caused the flash. They found none, supporting the neutron star merger idea. This discovery could help explain hundreds of mysterious fast X-ray transients — bright flashes from distant galaxies whose origins have puzzled astronomers. "It is an opportunity to have a front-row seat to the most extreme forces of the Universe," Passaleva said.
why_it_matters: Most cosmic explosions are over before anyone can study them, so a ten-minute X-ray flash gives astronomers a rare chance to watch a newborn object develop and may finally explain hundreds of mysterious cosmic flashes. It also connects to something physical: much of the gold and other heavy elements around us was probably forged in collisions exactly like this one.

background_read: Neutron star collisions are thought to be the universe's heavy-element factories, and most of the gold and platinum on Earth was probably forged in crashes like this one. In 2017, the LIGO and Virgo detectors (huge laser observatories in the United States and Italy that sense ripples in space) picked up gravitational waves from two neutron stars merging, letting astronomers study one event with both gravitational waves and light.

The Einstein Probe (a space telescope launched in January 2024, led by China with international partners) was designed to catch short X-ray flashes that other missions miss, and the Very Large Telescope (a group of giant mirrors on a mountain in Chile's Atacama Desert, run by the European Southern Observatory) followed up from the ground. Eleonora Troja (an astrophysicist who studies neutron star mergers and their afterglows) is a co-author of the study in Science Bulletin, a peer-reviewed science journal.

A magnetar is the most magnetic kind of neutron star known: its field is far stronger than anything humans can produce, and it can flood the galaxy with radiation as it spins down. Because this flash lasted ten minutes instead of two seconds, the team argues that something kept feeding it energy — the signature they expected from a newborn magnetar.

perspectives.description: For researchers who study neutron stars, this event is the strongest hint yet that mergers can leave behind a magnetar. It also gives them a new way to think about the hundreds of fast X-ray transients that have never been explained.

A single event is a clue, not proof. Other processes, such as leftover material falling back onto the merged object or a jet pointed in an unusual direction, could also stretch a flash to ten minutes. These researchers will want several more events showing the same pattern before accepting the magnetar story.

The real shift here is technological: wide-field X-ray monitors such as the Einstein Probe, combined with fast ground-based follow-up, are turning rare one-off events into a population that can be studied statistically. That is how a strange anomaly becomes a normal class of object.

If more ten-minute X-ray flashes turn up without a supernova, ideas about how magnetars form will need rewriting, and gravitational-wave detectors may one day catch a merger at the same moment. If they do not, EP250704a may become a warning about reading too much into a single signal.
